manuscript_meta.title: LIE-ACCESS NEURAL TURING MACHINES Greg Yang and Alexander M. Rush {gyang@college,srush@seas}.harvard.edu Harvard University

report.summary: This paper introduces Lie-Access Neural Turing Machines (LANTMs), a novel architecture for external neural memory. The core idea is to replace the common practice of creating 'soft' differentiable versions of discrete memory structures (like tapes or stacks) with a memory access mechanism grounded in the mathematics of Lie groups. The authors argue that Lie groups naturally provide desirable properties for relative indexing—differentiability, invertibility, and identity—which are lacking in some existing models. The proposed LANTM uses a controller to generate Lie group actions (e.g., shifts, rotations) that move a continuous head over a key-space manifold. Experiments on a range of algorithmic tasks demonstrate that LANTM and its spherical variant (SLANTM) outperform baselines, including standard LSTMs and simplified NTMs, particularly in generalizing to longer sequences. The work is supported by compelling qualitative analysis showing the models learn intuitive geometric data structures.

points: The central contribution—using Lie groups to formalize differentiable relative memory access—is highly original and theoretically elegant. It provides a principled mathematical foundation for a problem often addressed with ad-hoc 'softening' techniques.

The paper convincingly argues why properties like invertibility are important for relative addressing and demonstrates that existing popular models may lack them, thus clearly motivating the need for a new approach.
The experimental setup is strong, testing the models on a diverse set of algorithmic tasks that effectively probe memory and generalization capabilities.
The inclusion of a generalization test on 2x length sequences is crucial and provides strong evidence for the proposed model's effectiveness over baselines, which largely fail this test.

The qualitative analysis presented in Figures 2, 3, and 4 is excellent. It offers valuable insight into the model's internal workings, visually demonstrating that the LANTM learns continuous representations of discrete data structures (e.g., lists, sorted arrays) as hypothesized.
The paper is very well-written and structured. Complex mathematical concepts (Lie groups, manifolds) are introduced intuitively and are well-connected to the application domain.
The figures and tables are clear and effectively support the paper's claims. The visualizations of the memory access patterns are particularly insightful.

The reference list requires a thorough review and correction. A significant number of citations are malformed or incomplete, making it difficult to locate the cited works. This detracts from the paper's scholarly quality and must be fixed for publication.

The paper notes that the current implementation has unbounded memory growth, which is a practical limitation for long-running tasks. While potential solutions are mentioned in the discussion, they are speculative and not implemented. An experimental demonstration of even a simple memory management strategy would significantly strengthen the work.

The observation that models trained on the large sample set sometimes generalize worse than those trained on the small set is intriguing but not fully explored. A deeper analysis of this overfitting phenomenon would be beneficial.

The appendix experiments with 'action interpolation' show mixed results. A more integrated discussion of this mechanism and why it helps on some tasks but hurts on others (e.g., LANTM on ODD FIRST) would add value.

detailed_comments.comment: The bibliography needs significant revision for accuracy and completeness. As confirmed by the evidence pack, 17 out of 20 references could not be automatically resolved, indicating a systemic formatting issue. Several entries appear to conflate details from different papers. For example, reference [2] lists metadata for Graves et al. (2016) but provides an arXiv URL for Graves et al. (2014). Similarly, reference [6] lists authors Joulin & Mikolov but its metadata (DOI, etc.) resolves to Hochreiter & Schmidhuber (1997). Please conduct a thorough review of the entire reference list to ensure every entry is accurate, complete, and correctly formatted for the camera-ready version.

The performance degradation with the larger training set on some tasks is a key finding that warrants more discussion. The paper suggests the model finds an algorithm that only works for training sizes. Could you provide more analysis? For instance, does the learning curve show a clear peak and subsequent decline in generalization performance? Does this suggest a need for different regularization strategies when training on larger, more varied datasets?

The discussion on unbounded storage is brief. To bolster the claim of this being a general-purpose mechanism, it would be very helpful to see an experiment with a memory constraint. For example, implementing a simple Least Recently Used (LRU) eviction policy, as mentioned, and showing that the model can still solve a task (perhaps with some performance trade-off) would make the framework's practical potential much more concrete.

questions: Could you please clarify and correct the discrepancies in the bibliography, particularly for entries [2] and [6], which appear to merge details from multiple sources?

The qualitative analysis of successful runs is a major strength. Have you analyzed the memory access patterns for failure cases? What do the learned geometric structures look like when the model fails to generalize correctly?

You note that a simple tape mechanism added little to the RAM baseline, yet your LANTM models show significant gains. Do you attribute this performance leap primarily to the guaranteed invertibility and identity properties of the Lie group structure, or are other factors, such as the choice of weighting function (inverse-square vs. softmax), equally critical?

Regarding the combination with random access (Section 4.3), how important was this component? Have you run an ablation study without the random-access interpolation to quantify its contribution to the final performance?
report.overall_assessment: This is a strong, innovative, and well-executed paper that introduces a novel and promising approach to neural memory. The core idea of using Lie groups is theoretically sound and the empirical results are compelling, particularly the demonstrated generalization capabilities. The qualitative analysis provides excellent insight and strongly supports the paper's narrative. The work has the potential to inspire a new direction of research in memory-augmented networks. We recommend this paper for acceptance, contingent on the authors addressing a few key issues for the camera-ready version. The most pressing issue is the state of the bibliography, which contains numerous errors and requires a complete overhaul for scholarly rigor. Additionally, the paper would be substantially strengthened by a more concrete discussion and, if possible, experimental analysis of the model's scalability (i.e., the unbounded memory issue) and a deeper investigation into the observed overfitting on larger datasets. Addressing these points will ensure the final paper is as impactful as its core contribution.

This paper introduces Lie-Access Neural Turing Machines (LANTMs), a novel architecture for external neural memory. The core idea is to replace the common practice of creating 'soft' differentiable versions of discrete memory structures (like tapes or stacks) with a memory access mechanism grounded in the mathematics of Lie groups. The authors argue that Lie groups naturally provide desirable properties for relative indexing—differentiability, invertibility, and identity—which are lacking in some existing models. The proposed LANTM uses a controller to generate Lie group actions (e.g., shifts, rotations) that move a continuous head over a key-space manifold. Experiments on a range of algorithmic tasks demonstrate that LANTM and its spherical variant (SLANTM) outperform baselines, including standard LSTMs and simplified NTMs, particularly in generalizing to longer sequences. The work is supported by compelling qualitative analysis showing the models learn intuitive geometric data structures.

findings.title: Lie-Access Bellek Yapısının Önerilmesi
findings.summary: Makale, mevcut nöral bellek sistemlerinin göreceli indeksleme için belirli bir yapıdan yoksun olduğunu savunarak, Lie gruplarına dayalı yeni bir bellek erişim mekanizması olan Lie-access belleği önermektedir. Bu yaklaşım, geleneksel ayrık bellek yapılarının (Turing makineleri gibi) temel özelliklerini (tersinirlik, özdeşlik) korurken farklılaşabilirlik sağlar.

manuscript_anchors.quote: In this work, we argue that these neural memory systems lack speciﬁc structure important for relative indexing, and propose an alternative model, Lie-access memory, that is explicitly designed for the neural setting. In this paradigm, memory is accessed using a continuous head in a key-space manifold. The head is moved via Lie group actions, such as shifts or rotations, generated by a controller, and memory access is performed by linear smoothing in key space. We argue that Lie groups provide a natural generalization of discrete memory structures, such as Turing machines, as they provide inverse and identity operators while maintaining differentiability.

We propose instead a class of memory access techniques based around Lie groups, i.e. groups with differentiable operations, which provide a natural structure for neural memory access. By deﬁnition, their differentiability satisﬁes the concerns of Criterion A. Additionally the group axioms provide identity, invertibility, and associativity, all of which are desirable properties for a relative indexing scheme (Criterion B), and all of which are satisﬁed by standard Turing machines. Notably though, simple group properties like invertibility are not satisﬁed by neural Turing machines, differentiable neural computers, or even by simple soft-tape machines.

manuscript_anchors.quote: External neural memory structures have recently become a popular tool for algorithmic deep learning (Graves et al., 2014; Weston et al., 2014). These models generally utilize differentiable versions of traditional discrete memory-access structures (random access, stacks, tapes) to provide the storage necessary for computational tasks. In this work, we argue that these neural memory systems lack speciﬁc structure important for relative indexing, and propose an alternative model, Lie-access memory, that is explicitly designed for the neural setting.

Recent work on neural Turing machines (NTMs) (Graves et al., 2014; 2016) and memory networks (MemNNs) (Weston et al., 2014) has repopularized the use of explicit external memory in neural networks and demonstrated that these networks can be effectively trained in an end-to-end fash-ion.

In this work, we introduced Lie-access memory, a novel neural memory architecture that uses Lie group actions to provide differentiable relative indexing. We showed that this approach is able to learn a variety of algorithmic tasks, often outperforming existing neural memory systems.
